metadata.title: Deep Half Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Deep Half Guard Bottom position in BJJ. Complete guide covering sweeps, back takes, and transitions. Defensive position with 60% sweep success rate at advanced level.

overview:
Deep Half Guard Bottom is an advanced guard position where the bottom player wedges underneath the opponent's hips with deep underhook control of the far leg. This position creates powerful leverage for sweeps and back takes by controlling the opponent's base from below. The bottom player's head is positioned near the opponent's far hip, with their body inverted underneath, creating a stable platform for offensive attacks.

This position is particularly effective against pressure passers who commit their weight forward, as it uses their momentum against them. The deep underhook of the far leg combined with the wedge created by the bottom player's shoulder and head disrupts the top player's base completely. From here, the bottom player can execute powerful hip-lift sweeps, waiter sweeps, and transitions to the back.

Deep Half Guard Bottom requires excellent hip mobility, core strength, and timing to enter and maintain. While it appears defensive, it is actually a highly offensive position with multiple pathways to dominant positions. The position is a cornerstone of modern no-gi grappling and has been refined by practitioners like Jeff Glover, Lucas Leite, and Bernardo Faria into a comprehensive attacking system.
state_invariants: Bottom player's head positioned near opponent's far hip, creating a wedge point with the shoulder pressed against the opponent's inner thigh
Deep underhook of opponent's far leg with bottom player's arm wrapped around the thigh, controlling the leg close to the body
Bottom player's body inverted underneath opponent's hips with shoulders and upper back on the mat, legs positioned to create leverage
Opponent's near leg typically controlled or monitored by bottom player's free hand or legs to prevent step-over passes
Bottom player's hips mobile and ready to elevate, creating constant pressure on opponent's base and balance

Bottom player able to create space to slide underneath opponent's hips
Deep underhook established on opponent's far leg before fully committing to position

Hip mobility to invert and maneuver underneath opponent's base

Keep head and shoulder wedged against opponent's inner thigh to disrupt their base
Stay inverted underneath opponent's hips to maximize leverage for sweeps
Control or monitor opponent's near leg to prevent step-over escapes
Use hip elevation and movement to keep opponent off-balance and reactive

common_errors.error: Losing deep underhook of far leg by allowing opponent to pull leg back
common_errors.consequence: Loss of primary control mechanism, making sweeps impossible and allowing easy pass
common_errors.correction: Maintain tight grip on far leg with arm wrapped deep around thigh, constantly pulling opponent's leg toward your chest

common_errors.error: Staying flat on back instead of inverted underneath opponent
common_errors.consequence: Reduced leverage for sweeps, easier for opponent to apply crossface pressure and pass
common_errors.correction: Keep shoulders and upper back on mat with hips elevated, body inverted underneath opponent's center of gravity

common_errors.error: Failing to control or monitor opponent's near leg
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily step over near leg and pass to mount or side control
common_errors.correction: Use free hand or legs to control opponent's near leg, preventing step-over escapes

common_errors.error: Remaining static without creating movement and angles
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can establish stable base and defend sweeps easily
common_errors.correction: Constantly shift hips, elevate, and create angles to keep opponent off-balance and reactive

common_errors.error: Attempting sweeps without proper setup or timing
common_errors.consequence: Failed sweep attempts expose back and allow opponent to pass easily
common_errors.correction: Wait for opponent to commit weight or react to feints before executing sweeps with proper leverage

common_errors.error: Allowing head to be too far from opponent's far hip
common_errors.consequence: Loss of wedge point, reduced sweep leverage, easier for opponent to escape position
common_errors.correction: Keep head and shoulder pressed against opponent's inner thigh near far hip, maintaining tight wedge

common_errors.error: Not transitioning when opponent escapes underhook
common_errors.consequence: Stuck in bad half guard with opponent achieving dominant position
common_errors.correction: Immediately transition to X-Guard, Half Guard, or re-establish position when underhook is threatened

expert_insights.danaher: Deep half guard represents a fundamental shift in guard philosophy - rather than controlling from the front, we control from below by removing the opponent's base entirely. The deep underhook of the far leg is non-negotiable; without it, the position ceases to function. The biomechanical advantage comes from creating a wedge with your shoulder and head against their inner thigh while maintaining an inverted position that allows you to lift their entire weight with your hips and core. Most beginners make the mistake of staying too flat - you must be inverted underneath their center of gravity to generate proper leverage. The position is a complete system with multiple sweep variations, but they all rely on the same fundamental principle: controlling the far leg while using hip elevation to disrupt their base. When entering, timing is critical - you need their weight committed forward before sliding underneath. The transition to back control via the rolling back take is particularly high percentage because it uses their defensive reactions against them.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Deep half guard is one of the most reliable positions in competition, especially in no-gi where it's harder for opponents to establish grips to defend. I use it constantly when facing heavy pressure passers who want to smash - the harder they drive forward, the easier the Homer Sweep becomes. The key is not to force the position too early; wait until they commit their weight, then slide underneath and establish the deep underhook. From there, I have four or five different sweeps I can hit depending on how they react. If they whizzer, I go to electric chair. If they post out wide, I hit the old school. If they try to step over, I take the back. The position is basically a trap - every defensive option they have opens up a different attack for me. In competition, I look for deep half especially after failed passing attempts when opponents are off-balance and looking to recover. One mistake I see all the time is people giving up the underhook too easily - you need to fight like hell to keep that far leg controlled because once it's gone, the position is finished.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Deep half guard is straight-up one of the most powerful positions in jiu-jitsu, period. We've built an entire system around it in 10th Planet because it works at the highest levels and it's nearly impossible to shut down if you know what you're doing. The beautiful thing is that it's a position where you can be completely underneath someone and still be attacking - that's the mind game aspect that freaks people out. They think they're winning because they're on top, but really they're in your trap. The electric chair from deep half is money - when they whizzer to defend the sweep, boom, you've got the lockdown locked in and you're attacking their knee. Jeff Glover really pioneered this position in no-gi and showed everyone how deadly it could be. The key is staying loose and mobile underneath - you can't be stiff or you'll get smashed. You need to be able to move your hips, change angles, and create that elevation for the sweep. We drill this constantly because the entry timing is everything. Too early and they'll defend, too late and they'll have already passed. But when you time it right and get that deep underhook, you're in complete control even though you're underneath.

metadata.title: Deep Half Guard | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Deep Half Guard in BJJ. Complete guide covering setup, control, escapes, and transitions. Success rates: Beginner 55%, Intermediate 70%, Advanced 80%.

overview:
Deep Half Guard is an advanced half guard variation where the bottom player positions themselves underneath one of the opponent's legs, creating a powerful leverage point for sweeps. Unlike traditional half guard where the opponent's leg is trapped between the bottom player's legs, deep half involves the bottom player getting their entire upper body underneath the opponent's center of gravity, often with the shoulder positioned at the opponent's far hip. This position offers exceptional sweeping leverage and is particularly effective for smaller practitioners against larger opponents.

The deep half guard represents a fundamental shift in guard philosophy, moving from traditional frames and distance management to an inverted leverage-based approach. By positioning underneath the opponent's center of gravity, the bottom player gains mechanical advantage that transcends size and strength differences. The position is characterized by extreme proximity and connection, with the bottom player using their entire body as a lever to disrupt the opponent's base. This creates opportunities for powerful sweeps that can lead directly to dominant positions or back control.

Successful deep half guard play requires excellent body awareness, hip mobility, and understanding of leverage mechanics. The position demands comfort in inverted and compressed spaces, as well as the ability to move dynamically while maintaining crucial connection points. When executed properly, deep half guard becomes a highly offensive position despite appearing defensive, offering consistent sweeping opportunities and entries to more advanced positions.
state_invariants: Bottom player positioned deeply underneath opponent's leg with upper body aligned near their far hip, effectively placing yourself under their center of gravity and disrupting their base from below
Inside arm actively underhooking opponent's trapped leg at the knee or thigh, securing it tightly with bicep and forearm pressure to maintain control and prevent extraction
Head strategically placed against opponent's hip or thigh, acting as a critical base point and leverage fulcrum, with neck and shoulder pressure maintaining structural integrity
Outside arm controlling opponent's far-side wrist, arm, or posting hand to prevent defensive framing and crossface attempts that could flatten the position
Hips remain mobile and active, positioned on the side or partially inverted, with legs framing or ready to push off the mat to create angles and generate sweeping momentum
prerequisites: Hip mobility and flexibility to invert and compress body underneath opponent
Comfort in inverted or underneath positions without panic or claustrophobia
Understanding of leverage and fulcrum mechanics for sweeping
Defensive awareness for counter-attacks including guillotines and crossface pressure
Ability to maintain connection while moving dynamically
key_principles: Position yourself underneath opponent's center of gravity with shoulder at far hip
Control opponent's knee or thigh with inside arm underhook and maintain tight connection
Use your head as a fifth limb for base and leverage against opponent's hip
Maintain connection to opponent's leg throughout all movement and transitions
Create and exploit leverage through deep underhooking position and hip movement
Prevent opponent from establishing crossface or head control with outside arm management
Use hip mobility to create angles and sweep opportunities while staying connected

common_errors.consequence: Leads to vulnerability to flattening as incorrect head placement allows opponent to crush your base and remove structural support
common_errors.correction: Position head strategically against their hip or thigh, using it as a base and leverage point to maintain structure and create sweeping fulcrum

common_errors.correction: Secure deep underhook on opponent's knee or thigh with tight bicep and forearm connection, pulling leg into your body to maintain control

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish crossface without outside arm defense
common_errors.consequence: Enables opponent to flatten you to mat and eliminate sweeping angles, neutralizing deep half guard effectiveness
common_errors.correction: Actively control opponent's far-side arm with outside hand to prevent crossface attempts and maintain ability to create angles

common_errors.error: Static hip positioning without active movement
common_errors.consequence: Creates stagnant position where opponent can stabilize base and begin methodical passing sequences
common_errors.correction: Maintain mobile hips that constantly adjust angles and create off-balancing momentum to keep opponent defensive

common_errors.error: Entering deep half without proper connection to opponent's leg
common_errors.consequence: Results in vulnerable position underneath opponent without leverage or sweeping capability
common_errors.correction: Establish firm underhook control before fully committing to deep half position, ensuring connection before inverting

common_errors.error: Failing to protect neck from guillotine attempts during entry
common_errors.consequence: Leaves you vulnerable to guillotine chokes as you dive underneath opponent's center of gravity
common_errors.correction: Keep chin tucked and posture strong during entry, controlling opponent's near arm to prevent guillotine grip

expert_insights.danaher: The deep half guard represents a sophisticated application of leverage mechanics that challenges conventional positional hierarchy. While I don't emphasize it as a primary position in systematic instruction, its mechanical validity cannot be dismissed. The position's effectiveness stems from precise biomechanical positioning - specifically the use of the head as a fifth limb creating a fulcrum point against the opponent's hip while the underhook controls the trapped leg. The key technical requirement is maintaining what I call 'structural connection' throughout all movement - the bottom player must never lose contact with the opponent's leg and hip, as this connection is the source of all sweeping power. The position works because it inverts the normal pressure dynamics of top-bottom relationships, forcing the top player to manage their base against leverage from underneath rather than simply applying downward pressure.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I use deep half primarily as a transitional weapon rather than a home base, particularly against opponents who pressure hard in half guard. The position gives you immediate sweeping threats that force opponents to react, and those reactions create openings for back takes and other advances. The critical detail most people miss is controlling the far-side arm - if your opponent can establish a strong crossface or posting hand, the position becomes much harder to maintain and sweep from. I also look for deep half entries when opponents are driving forward aggressively in half guard, using their own pressure against them. In competition, I find the Old School sweep and direct back takes from deep half to be the highest percentage options, with sweeps to mount being secondary. The position is especially effective in no-gi where the lack of grips makes it harder for opponents to control you once you're underneath.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Deep half is a fundamental component of the 10th Planet system, particularly in its integration with the lockdown and Electric Chair sequences. We've developed specialized variations that connect deep half to our unique control points and submission chains. The Jailbreak position, for example, uses deep half mechanics combined with lockdown control to create powerful sweeping leverage and Electric Chair submission opportunities. What makes our approach different is the emphasis on active control points - we don't just get underneath and hope for sweeps, we lock down the leg, control the far arm, and create systematic submission threats that force opponents into defensive reactions. The Twister system also incorporates deep half entries, particularly when transitioning from truck position. We practice deep half extensively with the rubber guard system, seeing it as part of an interconnected web of positions rather than an isolated technique. The innovation comes from connecting positions that traditional BJJ sees as separate into flowing sequences.

metadata.title: Deep Half Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Deep Half Guard Top in BJJ. Counter strategies, pressure maintenance, and passing opportunities. Beginner 35%, Intermediate 55%, Advanced 70%.

overview:
Deep Half Guard Top is a challenging defensive position where you find yourself on top but with your opponent underneath in deep half guard, meaning they have wedged themselves deep under your hips with their arms around your far leg and their head/shoulders positioned under your near hip. While you are technically "on top," this position presents significant sweep dangers and requires careful defensive strategy to maintain position and create passing opportunities.

The position is deceptive because the top player appears to be winning, but deep half guard is actually a highly effective sweeping position for the bottom player. Your opponent's deep positioning under your hips creates powerful leverage for sweeps, particularly the "Homer Simpson" sweep and waiter sweep, which can easily result in mount or back control for them if you don't defend correctly.

Success from top position requires understanding the sweep mechanics your opponent is attempting, maintaining proper weight distribution to counter these sweeps, and systematically working to extract your trapped leg and establish dominant passing pressure. Patience is essential, as rushing to pass without proper defensive positioning often results in sweeps or, worse, back exposure.
state_invariants: Opponent is positioned deep underneath your hips with their body inverted or perpendicular to yours, their shoulders and head creating a wedge under your near-side hip while they control your far leg with their arms wrapped around the thigh or knee
Your trapped leg is controlled by opponent's arms with their shoulder pressure preventing easy extraction, while your free leg maintains base contact with the mat to prevent being swept

Weight distribution is balanced between both legs to prevent opponent from utilizing leverage to execute sweeps, with your torso maintaining upright or slightly forward posture to avoid being flattened

Opponent's head position is underneath or beside your hip creating the fulcrum for potential sweep mechanics, requiring constant monitoring and defensive adjustment to prevent activation of sweep leverage
prerequisites: Opponent has successfully entered deep half guard from half guard bottom, lockdown, or open guard recovery
Opponent has established deep positioning with their shoulders underneath your hips and secured control of your far leg
You are on top but with compromised base due to opponent's deep underhook and hip positioning
Opponent has created the leverage structure necessary for sweep attempts while you maintain some degree of upright posture
key_principles: Weight Distribution Management: Maintain balanced weight—neither too far forward nor too far back—to prevent both types of deep half sweeps
Trapped Leg Extraction Priority: Systematically work to free your trapped leg as it's the key to escaping and establishing passing pressure
Crossface Control: Establish crossface or head control to limit opponent's ability to look up and execute sweep mechanics properly
Posture Maintenance: Keep good posture and avoid being flattened or broken down, which facilitates their sweeps
Base Widening: Use free leg to establish wide base that makes you difficult to off-balance
Grip Fighting: Prevent opponent from establishing waiter sweep grips (belt, pants) or underhook deep on your trapped leg
Patience Under Pressure: Recognize this is dangerous position requiring methodical escape rather than explosive attempts

common_errors.error: Explosive or forceful movements to free trapped leg
common_errors.consequence: Creates off-balancing forces that facilitate sweeps. Opponent uses momentum against you for Homer Simpson or waiter sweep, often resulting in being swept to mount or having back taken
common_errors.correction: Remain calm and methodical. Work gradual leg extraction while maintaining proper weight distribution and base. Small, controlled movements rather than big explosive ones. Focus on crossface first, then leg extraction. If frequently getting swept from deep half when attempting to escape, you're moving too explosively

common_errors.error: Incorrect weight distribution (too far forward or too far back)
common_errors.consequence: Placing too much weight forward enables waiter sweep; too much weight back enables Homer Simpson sweep. Poor weight distribution is primary cause of sweeps from deep half top
common_errors.correction: Maintain balanced weight distribution—roughly 50/50 or slight preference forward with proper base. Constantly monitor and adjust based on opponent's sweep attempts. Widen base with free leg to create stability. Feel where opponent is generating leverage and adjust accordingly

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to maintain head position deep under hip without pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent's head acts as fulcrum for sweep mechanics. Without disrupting this position, all their sweeps become high-percentage. Gives opponent time to establish perfect grips and positioning
common_errors.correction: Immediately establish crossface or head control to flatten opponent and disrupt their ability to look up. Use forearm or hand to apply pressure on their head, pushing it away from centerline. This breaks the sweep mechanics before they can develop

common_errors.error: Narrow base with free leg positioned close to body
common_errors.consequence: Makes you easy to off-balance and sweep. Limited base means any leverage opponent applies will move you. Essentially standing on one leg in unstable position
common_errors.correction: Widen base dramatically with free leg, posting it far to the side. Think tripod stance with free leg, trapped leg, and posting hand/arm creating wide stable base. The wider the base, the more force opponent needs to sweep you

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish waiter sweep grips without fighting them
common_errors.consequence: Once opponent has belt grip or pants grip for waiter sweep, the sweep becomes very high-percentage. These grips give them control of your upper body and ability to manipulate your weight distribution
common_errors.correction: Active grip fighting to prevent waiter sweep grips. If they establish grip, immediately strip it before they can execute sweep. Use two-on-one grip breaks. Recognize waiter sweep grip as immediate danger requiring response

common_errors.error: Staying in deep half top too long without systematically working to improve position
common_errors.consequence: Time favors the bottom player in deep half. The longer you stay, the more opportunities they have to perfect their grips, adjust positioning, and execute sweeps. Energy drain from maintaining defensive posture
common_errors.correction: Have systematic escape plan and execute it methodically. Don't accept staying in deep half indefinitely. Work crossface, base establishment, leg extraction, and pass in sequence. If one path blocked, switch to alternate escape but maintain forward progress

expert_insights.danaher: Deep half guard top represents one of the most deceptive positions in grappling—you appear to be winning because you're on top, but the reality is quite different. The bottom player has created a sophisticated lever system using your body weight against you, with their shoulders acting as the fulcrum underneath your hips. Understanding the biomechanics of the two primary sweeps from deep half—the waiter sweep and the Homer Simpson sweep—is essential for defensive success. The waiter sweep activates when your weight shifts too far forward, allowing them to lift and rotate you over their shoulder. The Homer Simpson sweep works when your weight is too far back, enabling them to roll you backward over your own base. Your defensive strategy must center on weight distribution that negates both sweep mechanisms simultaneously, which requires balanced positioning with neither too much forward nor backward lean. The systematic escape involves establishing a crossface to disrupt their vision and sweep mechanics, widening your base with the free leg to create stability, and methodically extracting the trapped leg while maintaining proper weight distribution. This is not a position for explosive movements—every sudden motion creates momentum that skilled practitioners will redirect into sweep attempts.
